## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The Diṭṭhisaṁyutta ("Linked Discourses on Views", SN 24; PTS S III 204–216) is the twenty-fourth section of the Saṁyuttanikāya, situated in the Khandhavagga [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Devdas 2004]. It contains 96 discourses methodically organized across four cycles or "trips" (*gamana*) on speculative views (*diṭṭhi*), differing principally in their overarching analytical framing formulas [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003]. Modern scholars identify the collection as an extension or appendix to the *Khandhasaṁyutta* (SN 22), elaborating its *Diṭṭhivagga* by systematically examining the origin of views through the lens of the five aggregates (*khandha*) [Bodhi 2003; Sujato 2012]. Within the genre classification found in the *Yogācārabhūmiśāstra*, it is reckoned as *vyākaraṇa* (expositions) [Sujato 2012].

The central teaching of the saṁyutta is that all speculative views and heresies arise conditioned by grasping and clinging to the five aggregates or empirical personality (*sakkāya*) [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Perez-Remon 1980]. Employing a structured question-and-answer format, the Buddha addresses a wide spectrum of views, ranging from determinism and moral skepticism to classic cosmological tenets concerning whether the world or the soul is eternal, finite, or distinct from the body [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Perez-Remon 1980]. Notably, the opening discourse (SN 24.1, *Vātasutta*) presents a unique philosophical stance asserting that winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, and all things remain immovably fixed like a pillar (*esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhita*)—a doctrine denying the reality of change affiliated with Pakudha Kaccāyana and early Ājīvikism [Bodhi 2003; Perez-Remon 1980]. Views are further shown to arise from clinging to things perceived, searched for, and pondered over by the mind (*manasā*) [Devdas 2004].

SuttaCentral notes Chinese parallels in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99; e.g., SĀ 142, 152, 154–164, 166, and 168), reflecting a parallel sequence where discourses on views follow the aggregate section [SuttaCentral; Sujato 2012]. DharmaNexus aligns the text with multiple fascicles of T 99, the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100), Sanskrit works including the *Avadānaśataka*, the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, as well as Tibetan Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records over 10,000 shared passages across 154 texts, with the closest reuse found in the *Khandhasaṁyutta* (SN 22), the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), the *Abyākata Saṁyutta* (SN 44), and Majjhima Nikāya discourses including MN 22 (*Alagaddūpama Sutta*), MN 76 (*Sandaka Sutta*), and MN 146 (*Nandakovāda Sutta*) [DharmaNexus].
